articles.title: 'Over-Under' Predictions for Every NBA Team's Final 2026-27 Record
articles.summary: We've reached the point in the NBA offseason where attention shifts from tracking transactions to assessing how all those moves might change the balance of power in the league.
articles.body:
We've reached the point in the NBA offseason where attention shifts from tracking transactions to assessing how all those moves might change the balance of power in the league.

It's already clear that lottery reform feels different this time around.

The overs are all more tempting than they should be, but maybe that's based on how things used to work. Do oddsmakers wrongly think new lottery odds will create parity, suppress tanking and make it so teams you'd normally pick to win 50 games fall closer to 45? Is it even possible for anyone to finish with a win total in the teens anymore?

It's very difficult to predict how clubs will behave when they no longer have an incentive to lose games late in the year. What happens when the pushovers actually push back in March and April?

Will the San Antonio Spurs and Oklahoma City Thunder both crack 60 wins? Will lottery reform eliminate tanking and ensure nobody loses 60?

ATL | BKN | BOS | CHA | CHI | CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GSW | HOU | IND | LAC | LAL | MEM | MIA | MIL | MIN | NOP | NYK | OKC | ORL | PHI | PHX | POR | SAC | SAS | TOR | UTA | WAS

Marginally more talented and featuring key young players who could still take steps forward, the Atlanta Hawks are a perfect test case for how the new lottery rules could affect competitive balance.

Lu Dort, Aaron Wiggins, Ryan Nembhard and even rookie Kingston Flemings bring added depth to a roster that won 46 games last season.

Playoff struggles should have motivated Jalen Johnson to deepen his bag, Dyson Daniels can't possibly shoot 18.8 percent from three again, and Onyeka Okongwu's new spacing dimension has him on a path toward fringe stardom.

All those positives still count, but so does a lottery system that will make a late-season run like the one Atlanta enjoyed last year much tougher. Many of the wins during the Hawks' 18-2 stretch from Feb. 22 to April 3 came against Brooklyn, Washington, Milwaukee, Memphis and others who'd completely packed it in.

It won't be quite so easy to fatten up this time around, which makes the Hawks feel more like a 42-win team than one capable of hitting 44.

If Jaylen Brown's absence is a problem, it'll matter most in the playoffs. We don't care about that here.

A Boston Celtics team that won 56 games while posting the point differential of a 60-win squad last season should be expected to do at least that well if the only change were swapping a healthy Jayson Tatum into Brown's vacated role. An All-NBA nod was a big deal for Brown; it's the expectation for Tatum—even coming off injury.

When you factor in what the Celtics should get from new additions Paul George and Mitchell Robinson and note how head coach Joe Mazzulla ensures maximum buy-in at all times, it gets even easier to see them pushing past the 51 wins they'd need to hit their over.

Don't forget the likelihood that Derrick White remembers how to shoot after going cold all last season. Also, let's make sure to account for organic growth from Boston's youngsters. Jordan Walsh, Hugo Gonzalez, Baylor Scheierman and Ron Harper Jr. could all be better than they were in 2025-26.

The Brooklyn Nets will give a significant share of their playmaking responsibilities to new addition Julius Randle and rookie guard Mikel Brown Jr., neither of whom seems poised for success.

Randle was salary-dumped from the Minnesota Timberwolves largely because he wasn't good enough as a second option behind Anthony Edwards. Brown is bound to struggle as professional defenses key in on him. Though the Nets got good deals on role players like Keon Ellis (two years, $18 million), Day'Ron Sharpe (two years, $20 million) and Josh Minott (two years, $9 million), the supporting cast here is underwhelming.

Maybe the best way to frame it: Brooklyn has the lowest over/under total in the East. It'd have to win five more games than last year to hit the over. Even if head coach Jordi Fernandez continues to motivate at a high level, and even if the Nets have no incentive to tank with Houston controlling their 2027 first-rounder, the roster just isn't improved enough to climb the standings.

Trades That Should've Happened During NBA Offseason 🏀

It's easy to build the case for the Charlotte Hornets going under 38.5 wins. It seems like most observers are convinced LaMelo Ball's exit constitutes a conscious step backward for the organization, one taken in an Eastern Conference that looks loaded with improved teams.

Are we sure Coby White can't replace 85 percent of LaMelo's playmaking? What if Naz Reid's spacing, combined with steps forward from Brandon Miller and Kon Knueppel, produces offensive numbers nearly as good as last year's? The defense will certainly be stouter without Ball out there for teams to attack.

Suppose new additions Royce O'Neale and Grayson Allen combine to bring more value than the departed Miles Bridges? At the very least, they'll ensure the Hornets get up tons of threes.

It's probably a hot take to say Charlotte can win more than last year's 44 games without Ball, but they had a 53-win point differential to reach that total. The Hornets could get significantly worse and still crack 39 to hit the over.

Nicolas Claxton and Norman Powell give the Chicago Bulls more veteran firepower than they had last season, but that will only matter until one or both of them get traded.

Powell's deal is particularly designed to be moved. Chicago inked him to a two-year agreement worth $44 million, but the second season is a team option, presenting a trade suitor with the dual appeal of present production and future flexibility.

Everyone seems to agree that rookie Caleb Wilson has star potential, but even rookies with that kind of long-term upside tend to do more harm than good in their first seasons. Chicago should give Wilson all the playing time and responsibility he can handle, but it should also be prepared for him to hurt the bottom line.

A star leap from Matas Buzelis is the Bulls' best path to hitting their over, but heavy minutes for young players and the possibility of a sell-off make it safer to assume a win total in the high 20s.

One of several Eastern Conference teams clustered in this general range, the Cleveland Cavaliers look at least as good as they have at any point in the last four seasons. They've averaged 54 wins during that stretch.

Peyton Watson fills a critical void between the James Harden/Donovan Mitchell backcourt and the Evan Mobley/Jarrett Allen combo up front, providing athleticism, defense and secondary creation while also threatening opponents with a three-point shot that crept just over 40.0 percent last season.

Depth could be an issue with Dean Wade, Dennis Schroder, Max Strus and Keon Ellis heading out over the summer. Watson and the other starters will need to be in top form for the postseason, which could lead to a few "no hope" nights when several starters sit and the overmatched reserves slide into larger roles. Then again, Cleveland could get a breakthrough year from Jaylon Tyson. Sam Merrill is one of the most underrated backups in the league.

Cleveland probably can't and won't chase the 64 wins it reached in 2024-25, but 49 would be below its average over the last few seasons and should be a goal given the potential importance of seeding come playoff time.

Cooper Flagg's natural growth and Kyrie Irving's return should add five extra wins this season, but that would only take the Dallas Mavericks to a 31-51 record if we're working off last year's 26-56 mark.

New head coach Dusty May comes with all the usual questions about a college transplant. Generally speaking, these kinds of hires don't work out. If he succeeds in getting Dallas back into the thick of the playoff picture, he'll be the exception that proves the rule.

The glut at forward pairs with a dearth of playmakers, leaving Dallas a little unbalanced. Much depends on Irving getting back in form after his torn ACL. That's a tall order for a 34-year-old who could also start angling for a trade to a higher-level competitor at some point during the season.

The path to hitting the over features a rejuvenated Dereck Lively II, an expectation-beating coaching season from May, a healthy and happy Irving and sustained progress from Flagg. That last factor is the only one we should count as a given.

Even as they've sent out key players to save money, battled injuries to indispensable starters and scrambled to build a real defense around Nikola Jokić's limitations, the Denver Nuggets have almost always been good enough to threaten the 50-win mark.

Their worst 82-game record since Jokić stepped to the fore came in 2017-18, when they won 46 games.

Peyton Watson's absence saps the Nuggets of what little athleticism they had. The quieter departures of Tim Hardaway Jr. and Jonas Valanciunas contribute to perhaps the thinnest roster of the Jokić era.

If Aaron Gordon can't stay healthy, new addition DeMar DeRozan can't prop up bench units and "why not?" camp invitee Cam Whitmore doesn't impress, the Nuggets could wind up outside the West's top six.

In the end, it's just too hard to bet against Jokić, who'll ensure Denver posts the league's highest offensive rating whenever he's on the floor. If Jamal Murray, Cam Johnson and Gordon hold up while Christian Braun shakes off last year's injury issues, another 50-win season should be the expectation.

All the shooting the Detroit Pistons added over the offseason could help improve on last year's No. 10 finish in offensive efficiency , even if the team's failure to add more playmaking feels like a mistake.

Isaiah Stewart's absence from the reserve rotation could knock the Pistons down from their No. 2 perch in defensive efficiency, but Ausar Thompson should probably be good enough to offset some of that slippage. Or at least he'd better be, given the $155 million extension he signed.

Jalen Duren's potential unhappiness seems significant enough to warrant some attention. It's not a given that John Collins will be an upgrade over Tobias Harris at the 4.

Though we've spent most of this space outlining concerns, we need to remember that the Pistons won 60 games last year and are still led by MVP candidate Cade Cunningham. They could endure several bad breaks and still reach the 49 wins they'll need for the over.

If Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody were both fully healthy for the start of the season, and if Kristaps Porzingis were assured of playing in at least 60 games for the first time since 2022-23, and if anyone could be sure that the runner's knee that limited Stephen Curry to 43 games a year ago was gone for good, maybe you could feel safe picking the over.

Because none of those things are certain, it just doesn't make sense to predict that the Golden State Warriors will win at least two more games than they did last season.

Butler is 37 and coming off a torn ACL. Nobody's sure when he'll return, but it seems safe to assume he'll be further reduced athletically than he was before the knee injury. The Warriors cannot expect more overall production this season than he provided in 38 games a year ago.

An already ancient roster is a year older. The only new addition is rookie Yaxel Lendeborg, while the complete lack of playmaking beyond Curry puts even more pressure and attention on him.

There will be nights when Steph and the Dubs look like their old selves. There just won't be 39 of them.

Fred VanVleet won't be his best self at 32, coming off an ACL tear, but he'll at least help a Houston Rockets offense that relied on Kevin Durant to a ridiculous degree last year.

KD will still be central, but VanVleet's return, growth from Reed Sheppard, newcomer Marcus Smart and the hopeful emergence of Amen Thompson's offensive game could bring a more egalitarian approach to Houston's half-court attack. At the very least, it'll make the Rockets less predictable in close-and-late situations. Even modest improvements there should, combined with an excellent defense, make Houston a tough beat.

Steven Adams will still produce elite offensive rebounding rates whenever he's on the floor. Alperen Sengün may not be done developing his game at 24. Tari Eason will make an impact if he can stay healthy.

A 52-win team last year, the Rockets are objectively more talented this time around and still have a couple of players capable of making leaps. All told, it shouldn't be that hard to cruise past 47 wins for an easy over.

When we last saw a fully healthy version of the Indiana Pacers, they were tipping off Game 7 of the 2025 NBA Finals with a real shot to beat the Oklahoma City Thunder.

Tyrese Haliburton's Achilles blew out early in that contest. That led to a gap year that apparently made oddsmakers forget how good Indy once was.

Haliburton is back. The Pacers added bulk by trading for Ivica Zubac late last season, as one of the NBA's most dynamic offenses should be up and running once again. Indiana's 50 wins in that 2024-25 season might be tough to match without picking up a few cheap victories against tankers, but reaching 44 should be doable if Haliburton is even close to what he used to be.

The LA Clippers are without their three best players from last season, having sent Kawhi Leonard to Toronto in the offseason and shipping out James Harden and Ivica Zubac during the year.

An over/under figure this low makes it seem like LA didn't get anything back in those trades or sign new blood in free agency.

Darius Garland looked terrific for the Clips after coming over for Harden, averaging 19.9 points and drilling 43.8 percent of his threes in 19 games. Brandon Ingram, the main return for Leonard (draft picks excluded), is a low-end All-Star. Free agent forward Rui Hachimura can stripe it from deep.

The Clippers are almost certainly no better than a Play-In team. A Garland trade could bring the under into play if no helpful on-court pieces come back in that hypothetical. 29 wins just seems too low for a team with legitimate talent at key positions.

Let's pencil the Clippers in for 32 wins and move on.

There's at least a discussion to be had about whether the rebuilt Los Angeles Lakers that feature Walker Kessler, Sandro Mamukelashvili, Quentin Grimes, Collin Sexton, Matisse Thybulle and Ziaire Williams are actually better than last year's edition, which included LeBron James, Marcus Smart, Rui Hachimura, Deandre Ayton and Luke Kennard.

While that debate clearly means Los Angeles overspent in both cash and draft capital on its new roster, it doesn't point to a downgrade large enough to knock 9 wins off last year's total.

That's what it would take for the Lakers to hit the under here.

Much depends on Luka Dončić staying healthy enough to produce a top-five offense, but Austin Reaves provides some playmaking insurance in the event of injury. Assuming Kessler is good enough to prop up a mostly punchless defense, a win total in the high 40s seems realistic.

It's hard to know how organically bad the 2025-26 Memphis Grizzlies really were. Among the most egregious lineup manipulators and unabashed tankers in the league, the Grizzlies managed just 25 wins last season.

Even if Memphis could have won closer to 30 games with a real effort, the same lottery reform that disincentivizes them from losing so much on purpose this time around should make their competition tougher to beat.

Zach Edey's return to health and Cam Boozer's promising floor game give Memphis a front line worth respecting. The veteran duo of Isaiah Stewart and Jerami Grant adds real depth. If Cedric Coward takes a step toward stardom, the Grizzlies could be a tough team to beat on most nights.

In the end, we need to remember that Memphis is rebuilding, facing more focused competition and is mainly interested in player development. That's going to keep them below 29 wins.

The Miami Heat won 43 games and posted the point differential of a 47-win team last year. Adding Giannis Antetokounmpo is supposed to make them...worse?

It appears concerns about the Heat's depth and Antetokounmpo's age/injury risk are playing a big role here. It's reasonable to consider the downside. It still feels safer (and a lot more fun) to bet on a motivated Antetokounmpo putting together a season that lands him on the MVP shortlist while playing for the best coach in the league.

Klay Thompson and Tim Hardaway Jr. provide desperately needed spacing. There's the outline of a top-five defense, while the uptempo offensive system Miami installed last year seems to play right into Giannis' strengths as a downhill attacker in a spaced floor.

You can knock the Heat for mortgaging their future for what might be a brief stint as a fringe contender, but that's a long-term issue. Just looking at the upcoming season, Miami certainly seems capable of winning at least 44 games.

Taylor Jenkins will get more out of the Milwaukee Bucks than a mostly checked-out Doc Rivers did last season. The new head coach also has a deeper roster than most believe.

Milwaukee got back Tyler Herro, Kasparas Jakucionis, Jaime Jaquez Jr. and Kel'el Ware for Giannis Antetokounmpo. They'll join Ryan Rollins, Myles Turner, AJ Green and a handful of others to create a real NBA rotation. It's possible one or more of the Bucks' movable vets could be traded, which could suppress the team's win total. But the actual talent on hand is good enough to win 30 games.

In fact, it wouldn't be a complete shock if this year's Bucks bested the 32 wins produced by last season's team. At the very least, without Giannis' trade situation hanging over the franchise, the vibes in Milwaukee should be improved.

Nobody's predicting a postseason trip, but the Bucks aren't nearly as bereft of proven NBA players as some other teams near the bottom of the projected standings.

This year's Minnesota Timberwolves will be meaningfully different from the ones that won 49 games last season. Without Julius Randle and Naz Reid, the updated Wolves are built around a seemingly deep guard rotation that might not be built to pile up wins over the course of the year.

LaMelo Ball's spotty health record is a huge reason the Hornets moved on from him. One minute-managed 72-game season in 2025-26 doesn't erase the fact that he averaged 35 across the previous three years. If he misses significant time, Anthony Edwards will be even more strained on offense than he used to be, absent Randle's secondary playmaking and Reid's critical spacing.

This version of Minnesota, playing at full strength, might have a better chance to reach the Finals than previous ones. That should be the central focus in the wake of a bold, all-in trade. That's not the same thing as saying the Wolves are built to rack up 50 wins during the year.

The 62 games he played last season feel like the upper limit on expectations for Zion Williamson in the coming year. Even that might be optimistic; it was the second-highest total of his career.

The New Orleans Pelicans didn't exactly add much talent to offset Zion's potential absence. They also didn't meaningfully improve the roster that produced their 26-56 record in 2025-26.

Bennedict Mathurin is the Pels' only notable newcomer. His mostly empty scoring won't be all that helpful on a team that ranked worse on defense than on offense last season.

Maybe if new head coach Jamahl Mosley somehow coaxes league-average defensive work out of this group while Trey Murphy III pops and second-year duo Derik Queen and Jeremiah Fears take big steps forward, the over will be in danger.

Otherwise, the expectation should be something very close to last year's 26 wins.

Winning the 2026 NBA championship required historic comebacks and put the New York Knicks through heavy minute totals under intense pressure. They played 101 games between the regular season and playoffs and were battling it out with the San Antonio Spurs midway through June, a full two months after half the league had wrapped up their campaigns.

Then came the parades, interviews, media blitzes and all the rest of the exhausting post-title necessities.

With a core made up mostly of players who've crossed over to the wrong side of 30, and in the wake of everything they just went through, the Knicks are not exactly coming into the 2026-27 season with fresh legs and renewed spirits.

New York is a contender. Nobody is going to want a piece of it in the playoffs. But defending champs feel fatigue more acutely than anyone, which will keep the Knicks under 51 wins.

The Oklahoma City Thunder have averaged 63 wins per season over the last three years, topping out at a whopping 68 in 2024-25. Heading into the season, they're first-class contenders who could lead the league in wins if that's their priority.

A potentially shallower roster, the likelihood of resting a couple of key players more often and the dearth of tankers to smash in March and April should all prevent OKC from hitting the over.

Having shed Lu Dort, Aaron Wiggins and Isaiah Joe, the Thunder are down one starter and two rotation players. Cason Wallace, Jared McCain and Ajay Mitchell will more than offset those absences by playing bigger minutes in the playoffs, but Oklahoma City may not want to overtax them during the year. That'll result in some deeper-bench options receiving playing time, as the Thunder will also surely take it easy on Chet Holmgren, Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and especially Jalen Williams.

After enduring multiple hamstring injuries last season, J-Dub will find himself on ice for extended periods if he feels even the slightest tweak in that leg.

Expect younger options like Nikola Topić, Thomas Sorber, Bennet Stirtz and Aday Mara to see action as OKC conservatively manages its way through the year.

The Orlando Magic got just 408 possessions from their ideal starting lineup. They endured yet another unimaginative offensive season under fired head coach Jamahl Mosley and saw Paolo Banchero's jumper completely abandon him.

Other than the increased number of capable, competitive teams in the East, there's not much of a reason to believe the Magic are in for slippage.

New head coach Sean Sweeney almost has to be an improvement over Mosley. The Magic are going to get Banchero and Franz Wagner on the floor for an extended stretch at some point before both retire. Assuming even moderate health luck and a more dynamic attack under Sweeney—perhaps one driven by a resurgent Banchero who gets to play for a coach he actually likes—Orlando feels like a threat to push toward 50 wins.

We all know the health caveats attached to Joel Embiid, who has averaged 32 games per season in the three years since he won MVP. If he's available for half of the Philadelphia 76ers' games, it'll be a surprise.

LeBron James will turn 42 in December and probably shouldn't be counted on for more than the 60 games he managed last year.

That means Tyrese Maxey, Jaylen Brown and VJ Edgecombe will need to carry the load if the Sixers are going to do better than 50 wins.

This is a bet that those three will be nearly good enough to handle that on their own. That James and Embiid will chip in often enough to get Philly to at least 51-31.

Coming off a relatively lucky 45 wins after posting a 40-win point differential, the Sixers have to make some real gains. Embiid's slightly better health, plus the Brown/James combo replacing Paul George's modest contributions, is reason enough for optimism.

You could make a case that the Phoenix Suns will fall short of 40 wins by pointing to Mark Williams' injury and the possibility that Miles Bridges won't be an upgrade over Royce O'Neale and Grayson Allen.

The real case against the Suns shows up in their record against good teams last season. When Phoenix squared off against opponents with records of .500 or better, it went just 21-30. Assuming the Suns won't be able to fatten up on tankers as they did a year ago, it's pretty easy to imagine them finishing with a losing record.

If Khaman Maluach takes a big step forward, and if head coach Jordan Ott is able to summon the same level of defensive intensity for the second year in a row, the over could be in danger. But the smart money is on Phoenix taking a step back in the standings because they'll face tougher competition more consistently.

The positional mixture of the Portland Trail Blazers' talent doesn't make a ton of sense, but there's at least more of it.

The logjam at guard between trade acquisition Ja Morant, returning icon Damian Lillard, Scoot Henderson and Jrue Holiday will be tricky to navigate. Even in a best-case scenario where Morant regains his star form, it'll come at the cost of reps and responsibility for Henderson. Meanwhile, the potential backcourt of Morant and Lillard is as defensively untenable as any in the league.

The biggest issue with all those guards is that none of them should handle the ball more than star forward Deni Avdija. His downhill attacks draw fouls and open up threes for teammates. Portland's best sets put the ball in his hands.

In the end, trusting Portland to hit the over requires faith in Avdija's continued brilliance, head coach Micah Nori's rotation management and a step toward All-Defensive status for big man Donovan Clingan. This is one of the toughest lines on the board, but the Blazers have the pieces to hit the over if they can get organized.

The Sacramento Kings won eight of their final 18 games, finishing 22-60 last year. That feat doesn't seem repeatable.

Domantas Sabonis wants out , Zach LaVine has no future with the team, and head coach Doug Christie didn't do anything last year to inspire confidence that he can run a functional show on either end. Rookie point guard Darius Acuff Jr. is poised to take a ton of lumps as his team's primary shot-creator.

Between having the most capricious ownership group in the league, arguably the least talented roster and a performance last year that probably should have produced only 17 or 18 wins, the Kings are this season's best bet to finish with a win total in the teens.

We went with the under on OKC's 61.5 figure. Some of the same lack of tankers should make it tricky for the San Antonio Spurs to climb above their similarly high total.

The Spurs differ from Oklahoma City in that they're not established champs with mid-prime stars who might need some rest. Instead, San Antonio is built on young, ascendant talent that doesn't seem to come with "off" switches. Dylan Harper, Stephon Castle and Victor Wembanyama won't average 40 minutes per night, but they'll play as if they've got everything to prove.

All three of those players should be better than the versions that led the Spurs to the Finals. They'll get support from veteran newcomer Tobias Harris and returners De'Aaron Fox, Devin Vassell and Julian Champagnie.

The Spurs' recent history suggests they'll care a little more than the Thunder about securing the West's top seed and sending a message. That, plus Wemby's impossible-to-project ceiling, should be enough to get to at least 61 wins.

Unless you think Brandon Ingram and Gradey Dick help a team's regular-season bottom line more than Kawhi Leonard does, you kind of have to take the Toronto Raptors' over.

After racking up 46 wins with a 49-win point differential last season, the Raps sent two future firsts and a swap with Ingram and Dick to the Clippers for Leonard. Injury and availability risks will dog Leonard until his career is over, but just half a season's worth of appearances from him should produce as much value as Ingram did in 77 games last year.

If Jakob Poeltl can shake the injury bug himself, Scottie Barnes' ongoing ascent reaches All-NBA levels for the first time and Collin Murray-Boyles makes a play for All-Defensive honors, Toronto could nudge up past 50 wins.

Walker Kessler's departure in a sign-and-trade with the Lakers forced the Utah Jazz to pivot from their original plans, which featured Kessler at the 5 in a hulking front line alongside Jaren Jackson Jr. and Lauri Markkanen.

Utah couldn't refuse the two first-rounders and two swaps Los Angeles offered, but it's hard to argue the team is better in the short term with Jusuf Nurkić and Jaxson Hayes playing the minutes that would have gone to Kessler.

That said, 38 wins just doesn't seem out of reach for a Utah team that just extended rising star guard Keyonte George and should take the tank-inspired training wheels off Markkanen and the rest of the vets. They can also expect growth from Ace Bailey.'

Choosing the over depends on the belief that Utah has been playing with one hand tied behind its back for the last several years. That it was giving games away to improve its lottery position. It requires faith that Will Hardy can be one of the league's best coaches in games that actually matter, while Jackson can hold up for more minutes at center than he or Utah expected.

None of those are givens, but the Jazz have real talent on both ends of the floor and should relish the chance to finally unleash it all after holding back for so long.

The Washington Wizards are going to be a meaningfully different team than the one that won 17 games a year ago. Led by veterans Trae Young and Anthony Davis, they have a shot at doubling their 2025-26 win total to clear the over. That's a rare feat, but it wouldn't be without precedent.

The Rockets almost pulled it off from 2022-23 to 2023-24, when they went from 22 wins to 41. The Pistons nearly tripled their victory count (14 to 44) from 2023-24 to 2024-25.

At the same time, this is still a mostly young team that cannot assume all of its under-25 players will take leaps. Price in the possibility that Davis will be injured or traded, while sprinkling in some concerns about Young's ability to recapture his past form and the brutal competitiveness of the East; it becomes easier to doubt that the Wizards will reach 34 wins.

In a conference this tough, somebody has to lose some games.

articles.title: Bargain NBA Free Agents Who Can Still Help Every Team
articles.summary: When Jalen Duren finally agreed to the Detroit Pistons' five-year, $200 million offer, the 2026 offseason's final starting-caliber free agent was officially off the board.
articles.body:
When Jalen Duren finally agreed to the Detroit Pistons' five-year, $200 million offer, the 2026 offseason's final starting-caliber free agent was officially off the board.

In fact, the arrival of training camp means anyone still unemployed probably isn't even a sure-fire rotation option. As it is, most teams have more bodies in their facilities than they'll be legally allowed to carry into the season.

We turned over a whole bunch of stones to come up with a handful of players who, despite virtually every roster spot being spoken for, should still get serious looks. This is the last batch of viable free agents on the market.

None projects to be a big-minute option, but each is good enough to play a small role on anyone's roster.

2025-26 Stats: 8.0 PTS, 4.0 REB, 4.4 AST, 0.8 STL

Anyone signing Vince Williams Jr. to a camp deal will do so knowing he won't produce until late in the 2026-27 season. He's sure to miss a huge chunk of the campaign while recovering from a torn ACL suffered last February.

Unlike some of the other players we'll list, Williams remains unrostered strictly because of his health status. He put up 8.0 points and 4.4 assists per game last season and, more broadly, has tended to play his best when tasked with a real role. Back in 2023-24, Williams' second season in the league, he posted averages of 10.0 points, 5.6 rebounds and 4.4 assists in 27.6 minutes per game.

That was the only time in recent memory Williams was a regular starter, but his work for Memphis as a 23-year-old should have teams interested in what he might do when healthy again.

Much depends on Williams' long-range accuracy. He's at 32.2 percent from deep for his career but drilled 37.8 percent of his treys during that breakout year with the Grizzlies. If he can settle in as a league-average shooter, Williams will have much more to offer than several players currently in camp on Exhibit 9 deals around the league.

Even if he can't find his perimeter stroke, Williams will bring rugged defense against bigger players and just enough facilitation to make an impact.

2025-26 Stats: 2.4 PTS, 0.7 REB, 0.5 AST, 0.2 STL

All we know for sure is that Lindy Waters III isn't good enough to crack the Western Conference champion San Antonio Spurs' rotation. The 29-year-old wing has plenty to offer teams outside the contender class.

Waters did his most efficient work with the 2023-24 Oklahoma City Thunder, hitting 47.1 percent of his shots from the field and 43.5 percent of his threes in a small role across 38 games. The following season, which he split between the Golden State Warriors and Detroit Pistons, saw Waters appear in a career-high 52 games.

Though nobody should expect those excellent OKC shooting splits to reappear, Waters is at a solid 36.3 percent from deep for his career and has earned high praise from coaches who know a thing or two about what it takes to win.

"It's not just because he's a good shooter," Warriors head coach Steve Kerr said in 2024 . "He's a good basketball player. It's the shots that he doesn't take because of his patience, it's the cuts that he makes to the basket, it's getting into the fight defensively."

Waters has scrapped and clawed and spent plenty of time grinding in the G League since going undrafted in 2020. That he's logged nearly 200 career NBA games is a testament to his work ethic and the qualities—measurable and otherwise—he can bring to any team.

2025-26 Stats: 4.4 PTS, 1.4 AST, 1.0 REB, 0.5 STL

Like many players who establish themselves in South Beach, Gabe Vincent had a hard time recapturing his top form upon leaving the Miami Heat.

In four seasons with Miami, the 6'2" guard established himself as a useful defender and reliable shot-maker. Though he'll never be confused with a knockdown sniper, Vincent has been good for at least 34.0 percent from distance in three of the last five years.

Throw out an injury-plagued first season with the Lakers in 2023-24, and Vincent has also been durable, appearing in an average of 65 games over the last half-decade.

Some team in need of an experienced two-way guard who can get the ball up the floor, defend both backcourt spots and step into big shots without fear should put in a call to Vincent.

And if his decision to pass on a camp offer from the New York Knicks is any indication, that team had better be offering something more secure than a mere camp invite.

'Over-Under' Predictions for Every NBA Team's Record 🔮

Trades That Should've Happened During NBA Offseason 🏀

2025-26 Stats: 6.7 PTS, 5.8 REB, 1.8 AST, 0.4 STL

Kevin Love's All-Star peak is a decade behind him, but many of the skills that once made him one of the most complete offensive bigs in the game have predictably aged well.

In spot duty with the Utah Jazz last year, Love shot 37.3 percent from distance while averaging 12.6 rebounds and 3.9 assists per 36 minutes. He's obviously not going to touch that much playing time at age 38, but his per-minute production remains legit.

If anything, the veteran forward was a little too helpful for the tanking Jazz last season. Maybe he would have played more if Utah hadn't been 3.2 points per 100 possessions better overall and with him in the game.

You can just imagine the Jazz's front office noting how Love boosted the team's offensive rating by 6.9 points per 100 possessions (a 94th percentile figure) and immediately drafting a memo to the coaching staff limiting Love's role to 10 minutes per game.

Reliable shooting, intelligent ball movement, dominant rebounding and championship savvy play anywhere—even if only in an end-of-bench capacity.

2025-26 Stats: 7.1 PTS, 1.2 REB, 1.0 AST, 0.3 STL

Golden State's decision not to re-sign Seth Curry—even with Stephen Curry as the franchise cornerstone—suggests the Warriors did not view him as the right fit for their roster. That does not mean another team could not find value in his shooting, especially in a limited, matchup-dependent role.

Other teams should view the Dubs' decision as an opportunity. Stephen Curry signed an extension, but who knows how ugly things might get in Golden State this year? It might be a good idea to have Seth on your roster if you intend to swoop in with a trade offer for Steph at some point.

There's also the small matter of Seth being one of the absolute greatest shooters in the history of the sport.

Whatever issues Curry has with durability and defense—and there are issues in those areas—he has never once been anything but lights-out from deep. Though he barely played last season, he scorched the nets at a 48.0 percent clip from long range.

In 2024-25, when his 68 games with the Hornets qualified him for the crown, he led the NBA by shooting 45.6 percent on threes. Overall, his career hit rate of 43.3 percent is second all time among qualified shooters.

The league is evolving and continually favoring multi-skilled players with good positional size. But it hasn't advanced to a point where singularly elite skills like Curry's shooting are no longer valuable.

articles.title: 7 NBA Offseason Moves That Could Go Horribly Wrong
articles.summary: There's no such thing as a risk-free NBA transaction. Every trade and free-agent acquisition comes with downsides, but a few deals from the 2026 offseason just have more disaster potential than others.
articles.body:
There's no such thing as a risk-free NBA transaction. Every trade and free-agent acquisition comes with downsides, but a few deals from the 2026 offseason just have more disaster potential than others.

Many of the incredibly risky moves we're covering have reasonable justifications. If you have a shot to increase your championship equity with a trade, for example, it's often the right decision to go for it—even if it's not technically likely that the decision will pay off.

Here, we'll run through several swaps and signings that could go especially wrong for a variety of reasons. That's not to say these transactions are sure to fail. We're just highlighting the ones that could do the most damage if they don't work out.

The Charlotte Hornets will regret trading LaMelo Ball if he stays healthy and elevates the Minnesota Timberwolves to the contender class. But even if that happens, Charlotte will still have the first-rounders and players it acquired in the deal.

Minnesota, on the other hand, will be in a brutally tough spot if Ball doesn't deliver.

Consider: The Hornets just watched Ball enjoy the most productive season of his career and still chose to move on, despite having the most complete view of his health history, contract and the concerns about whether he can be the face of a winning franchise. Charlotte's decision is worth noting, particularly given the front office's track record under general manager Jeff Peterson.

If Ball proves he can stay on the floor for more than last season's 72 minute-managed appearances, elevate Minnesota's offense and answer questions about his defensive engagement and ability to lead a winning team, the Wolves will be thrilled with the deal.

If he falls short in any of those areas, Minnesota could be left questioning why it accepted so much risk for a player with Ball's injury history, expensive contract and uneven two-way track record.

Walker Kessler might be worth $130 million over four years. When last healthy, he graded out as one of the league's top offensive rebounders and rim protectors. Add a little offense to that profile, and it's not that hard to justify paying him like a top-10 player at his position.

Throw in the two unprotected first-rounders and two swaps the Los Angeles Lakers sent the Utah Jazz in the sign-and-trade to get Kessler, and the bar for his performance gets considerably higher.

Justifying that cost is probably beyond Kessler's ability. He'd need to stay healthier than he has in any of the last three years, land in the conversation for Defensive Player of the Year and help turn the Los Angeles Lakers into contenders.

Los Angeles paid a superstar price for a quality starter because it was desperate to support Luka Dončić with the kind of paint-patrolling, rim-rolling center he wanted. If this goes badly, a Lakers team that fired all its bullets at the wrong target could wind up losing Dončić to a team that can actually reach contender status.

You never want to be involved in a trade where everyone agrees the other side absolutely had to say yes.

No draft picks or prospects changed hands when the Washington Wizards acquired Trae Young for the expiring salary of CJ McCollum and the marginally underwater four-year, $54 million deal belonging to Corey Kispert last January.

Despite that trade signaling Young's relatively low value, the Wizards decided he was worth a four-year, $212 million max contract.

Washington attempted damage control almost immediately, leaking its belief that "Young would have commanded maximum-salary contract offers from other franchises," per Josh Robbins of The Athletic.

Few teams had enough cap space to give Young what Washington did, and ESPN's Zach Lowe nixed the notion that any of them were interested: "From what I know, it was not Brooklyn... Chicago has [Josh] Giddey. The Lakers have guards galore. The Pistons have Cade Cunningham and we're now out of teams with cap space. I don't know what they were afraid of or who they were bidding against."

Young is one of the worst defenders in the league, gives no off-ball value on offense and has never shed the reputation that "even the players who were eating off his passes didn't like him or enjoy playing with him," per The Athletic's John Hollinger .

If this contract deal was part of the price of acquiring Young in the first place, it was a mistake. If the Wizards fooled themselves into believing there was competition for him in free agency, even worse.

'Over-Under' Predictions for Every NBA Team's Record 🔮

Trades That Should've Happened During NBA Offseason 🏀

The Phoenix Suns shipped snipers Royce O'Neale and Grayson Allen to the Charlotte Hornets for Miles Bridges, who owns a career 33.8 percent mark from three.

If that were the entirety of the deal, it'd rate as a likely mistake for the Suns.

Bridges has posted net-negative defensive numbers throughout his career while almost always producing true shooting percentages below the league average . Considering he shared nearly 3,000 possessions with ace facilitator LaMelo Ball last year, Bridges' accuracy marks of 46.0 percent on twos and 33.3 percent on threes look pretty bad.

Bridges has also been dependent on his athleticism and could be in for decline as he enters his age-28 season. In fact, regression is already hitting. The percentage of his field-goal attempts at the rim has declined for five straight years.

Bridges is a borderline starter who could sign a huge extension while potentially hurting a Phoenix offense that needs its space.

Oh, and the Suns attached their unprotected 2033 first-rounder in the deal, coughing up their best future asset for a forward who probably won't make the team better on the floor this season.

The last time James Harden signed a contract or extension for longer than two years, he was a perennial MVP candidate playing for the Houston Rockets. In his travels since then—from Houston to Philly to Brooklyn to Los Angeles and now to Cleveland—no team has felt sure enough of his reliability to offer more than two guaranteed years.

The Cavs inked Harden to a fully guaranteed three-year, $97 million deal with a player option in 2028-29, his age-39 season.

What could go wrong? Other than the natural aging curve rendering Harden even less available and less effective defensively, his history of trade demands and his track record of postseason failures effectively capping Cleveland's ceiling at the Conference Finals?

Harden remains a very useful offensive player, and he's as durable as any late-30s star can be. But we know things tend to end badly when Harden sours on his circumstances, and Cleveland's championship-or-bust posture only further pressurizes the environment. Before this three-year deal is over, we're going to be reminded of why it's been so long since someone invested this heavily in Harden.

Based on the 8.1 points per game and 53.3 true shooting percentage he managed last season, Gary Trent Jr. isn't going to provide $64 million worth of production over the four years of his new contract.

But at around nine percent of the salary cap next year, Trent's deal isn't going to ruin the Milwaukee Bucks. They're rebuilding anyway, and they're already living with much bigger financial missteps than this one. For example, Damian Lillard will collect $21 million per season through 2029-30, and he hasn't played for the team in 18 months.

Overpaying Trent isn't a catastrophe, at least in part because the Bucks aren't built to win or maximize every dollar this coming season. It's the longer-term fallout they should be worried about.

Reports questioning whether Trent's deal complied with NBA salary-cap rules prompted the league to open an investigation , which could lead to further consequences if it finds a violation.

The charitable interpretation is that Trent's contract reflects Milwaukee's evaluation despite his recent production and prior, smaller salaries. A more concerning possibility is that the deal may have been arranged earlier than NBA rules allow—an issue the league is reportedly examining.

The Miami Heat can win the 2027 NBA championship with Giannis Antetokounmpo, and they couldn't have without him. Drill all the way down to that simple truth, and it justifies the trade that brought the two-time MVP to Miami for four quality players and virtually all of the draft capital the Heat could trade.

When you move past the binary "can vs. can't win a championship" style of analysis and think of Miami's situation probabilistically, the downsides become obvious.

It is certainly not likely that the Heat will win the title this season. In addition to a laughably loaded East, depth issues and the separate class of contenders out West (OKC and San Antonio), Miami's slim chance at success will vanish if Giannis declines or can't stay healthy for the regular season and playoffs.

Odds are, the Heat's massive trade won't yield a ring and may not even assure home-court advantage in the first round. Given the extent to which Miami mortgaged its future, you'd like to see more present promise.

articles.title: Fact check: Did Caitlin Clark make $29 million off-court move right after Indiana Fever’s playoff exit?
articles.summary: It is not surprising for Caitlin Clark to land stunning deals. She has earned her place as one of the most prominent faces of the WNBA.
articles.body: It is not surprising for Caitlin Clark to land stunning deals. She has earned her place as one of the most prominent faces of the WNBA. While Clark’s WNBA tenure is getting interesting, brands are rushing to sign her for endorsements. Recently, a rumor about the Fever guard’s huge paycheck surfaced, linking her to a whopping $29 million deal with audio streaming giant Spotify. Here’s the truth behind the rumor.Did Caitlin Clark sign a $20 million Spotify podcast deal?Caitlin Clark did not have a deal with Spotify. The rumor began with an X account called Fever Updates, which wrote: "Caitlin Clark has reportedly agreed to a $20 million deal with Spotify to launch a new exclusive podcast." The post added that the show would be weekly, would stream only on Spotify and would run through the start of the new WNBA season. It also promised a different guest every episode, drawn from the WNBA, the NBA and other industries.The claim fell apart on a basic check. As of now, no reliable outlet has reported a deal, and Clark's social handles have not announced anything about it. The post leaned on the word "reportedly" and gave readers nothing firmer.There is a reason the idea sounded believable. The three-time WNBA All-Star has a long break before returning to the floor with the Fever. A podcast would let Clark talk about things fans rarely hear during the season, and starting a show is the easiest way to do that. For now, Clark is not launching an exclusive show with Spotify.How can the Fever keep Clark happy after the early playoff exit?Indiana entered as the No. 6 seed, and the defending champion Las Vegas Aces closed the series in three games with a 94-83 win. Clark scored 18 points on 6-of-18 shooting and added four assists and two steals.Clark is under contract through 2027 after the Fever picked up the team option. Her All-WNBA honors in the first three years of the rookie deal also make her eligible to negotiate an EPIC extension. Linda Cohn, speaking on her own show, said the structure of that deal matters, including whether Clark would get an out if expectations are not met. On the roster, Cohn was blunt: "Indiana has to do more than pay its stars." She wants another perimeter defender next to Clark and more frontcourt help for Aaliyah Boston.The Fever star averaged 22.3 points, 4.0 rebounds and 8.3 assists this season, and all 44 regular-season Indiana games aired on national networks. Sophie Cunningham is an unrestricted free agent, and Kelsey Mitchell, the team's leading scorer, is headed toward free agency as well. Coach Stephanie White has pushed for a steadier defensive identity, pointing to the standard Tamika Catchings set. articles.title: Fired Trail Blazers announcer's legal team demands reinstatement after team axes him over teenage tweets
articles.summary: Braiden Bell's attorney is pushing the Portland Trail Blazers to reinstate the fired play-by-play announcer after tweets from age 15 resurfaced.
articles.body: Former Portland Trail Blazers play-by-play announcer Braiden Bell and his attorney are calling for his reinstatement after the team fired him hours after announcing his hiring over decade-old social media posts. Bell, 29, was hired from the WNBA’s Phoenix Mercury to replace Kevin Calabro, becoming the NBA’s youngest lead broadcaster. But the Blazers terminated his contract after tweets he wrote at age 15 resurfaced online. In December 2012, Bell tweeted, "I’m not racist at all.. But not gonna lie.. Asian people p— me off! Hahaha #Honest." In July 2013, he posted, "no blacks either. #racist." THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW! Bell retained sports employment attorney Arnie Herz, who previously represented San Antonio Spurs broadcaster Jacob Tobey in his reinstatement after a team suspension. In a statement provided to OutKick, Herz called for the Blazers to bring Bell back to the booth. "Should the worst words a fifteen-year-old ever wrote decide the rest of his life? That is the question now before the Portland Trail Blazers," the statement read in part. "Braiden is not asking anyone to excuse what he wrote. He has owned it, without excuses. What he is asking is whether a boy’s words from fourteen years ago should outweigh everything the man has done since. If that is the standard, there is hardly a person in any organization in America who could meet it. Accountability means owning what you did and showing who you have become. Braiden has done both." KARL RAVECH STUNS MLB FANS BY RETURNING TO ESPN BOOTH WEEKS AFTER BEING LAID OFF Bell also apologized for the posts in a statement. "I am deeply sorry for the language that I used on Twitter. These tweets, while wrong, were written by me 14 years ago while I was only 15 years old and have no reflection of who I am today. I do not take lightly any harm it causes now. I regret this being the first impression to many of you online, but I can take solace in knowing that the people who truly know me understand that this is not the kind of person I am. Again, I’d like to apologize to anyone who was hurt by my words and will continue to always treat people with kindness and respect." The Blazers fired Bell without placing him on administrative leave, citing team and league policies in a statement confirming the decision. "The Portland Trail Blazers have zero tolerance for racist, sexist, or harmful comments. Social media posts made by our recently announced play-by-play broadcaster are in clear violation of team and league policies, as well as our values and expectations. Therefore, we will not be moving forward with this broadcaster. The play-by-play role carries a long legacy of excellence, on the broadcast and in character, and we hold that standard without exception. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We did not meet our own bar in this process, and for that we apologize to Blazers fans and to Rip City. We believe strongly that everyone who is a part of Rip City should feel welcome and safe, and we will make sure that our new broadcaster reflects these values. We will do better." In response to the calls for reinstatement, the Trail Blazers reaffirmed their decision in a statement to The Athletic. "We stand by our statement issued last week and have no further comment at this time. We wish Mr. Bell the best." articles.title: La Euroliga decide seguir adelante con su expansión y la conversión de equipos en franquicias
articles.standfirst: Los 13 propietarios decidieron dar un paso trascendental para el baloncesto europeo en su Asamblea General en el Lago Como
articles.summary: Los 13 propietarios decidieron dar un paso trascendental para el baloncesto europeo en su Asamblea General en el Lago Como
articles.body: La Euroliga celebró este martes a orillas del Lago Como, en un búnker como la Villa d'Este, una Asamblea General trascendental. En ella se trataron temas de mucho calado para el futuro de la competición y del ecosistema del baloncesto en Europa. De hecho, los temas a tratar eran de enorme importancia, tales como la aprobación de un plan estratégico para la próxima década, la conversión en franquicias de las licencias, estudiar y admitir o no 13 propuestas de equipos que aspiran a formar parte de los socios de la Euroliga en una histórica expansión o el estudio de la oferta de NBA y analizar el estado de las negociaciones. En Cernobbio, los propietarios de los 13 equipos con licencia A de la Euroliga decidieron seguir adelante con el proceso de conversión de los equipos en franquicias y eso incluye a los 13 accionista de la competición: Anadolu Efes, Kosner Baskonia, CSKA, Armani Milan, Barcelona, Bayern Munich, Fenerbahce, ASVEL Villeurbanne, Maccabi Tel Aviv, Olympiacos, Panathinaikos, Real Madrid y Zalgiris Kaunas. Además la Euroliga va a seguir con su expansión. Los clubes acordaron continuar el proceso para ampliar el número de franquicias. Los propietarios de los clubes encargaron a la Junta Directiva proseguir con el proceso de evaluación y presentar una recomendación final para su aprobación en las próximas semanas, según el comunicado de la propia Euroliga. En cuanto a las neociaciones con la NBA y su oferta, no hay comunicación oficial de la Euroliga, pero la aceptación de seguir adelante con la conversión en franquicias y la expansión puede dar a entender que los 13 propietarios han rechazado ese ofrecimiento de la Liga estadounidense. Aunque no ha versión oficial.

articles.title: Tyson Pérez pasa por el quirófano y estará medio año de baja
articles.standfirst: El Unicaja sigue llenando su enfermería
articles.summary: El Unicaja sigue llenando su enfermería
articles.body: Tyson Pérez ya ha pasado por quirófano para solucionar sus problemas en el tendón de Aquiles de su pie izquierdo. El ala-pívot de Unicaja fue operado este lunes en Vitoria después de varias semanas arrastrando molestias en la zona que le habían impedido trabajar con normalidad. La intervención fue realizada por el doctor Mikel Sánchez, especialista en este tipo de lesiones, y se desarrolló de manera satisfactoria. El jugador cajista afronta ahora un largo proceso de recuperación que se prolongará aproximadamente seis meses. Tyson Pérez estará bajo la supervisión tanto del equipo médico que ha llevado a cabo la intervención como de los servicios médicos de Unicaja, que seguirán su evolución durante las diferentes fases de la recuperación. La lesión supone un importante contratiempo para el conjunto malagueño, que pierde durante buena parte de la temporada a uno de sus jugadores interiores. El objetivo ahora será que el ala-pívot complete su recuperación sin contratiempos y pueda regresar progresivamente a la actividad deportiva cuando los plazos médicos lo permitan. Aunque la previsión inicial apunta a aproximadamente seis meses de baja, los tiempos estarán condicionados por la evolución de la lesión y por la respuesta de Tyson Pérez al tratamiento y al proceso de rehabilitación. Su regreso a las pistas se producirá cuando esté completamente recuperado y pueda afrontar de nuevo la competición con garantías.

articles.title: John Collins grabs Dillon Brooks' throat mere minutes into Pistons-Suns preseason opener
articles.summary: It took less than five minutes for Brooks to rediscover his villainous ways, and for Collins to endear himself to the Pistons faithful.
articles.body:
If you found yourself wondering how long it would take Dillon Brooks to shake off any offseason rust and rediscover his customary villainous rhythm, or how long it would take newcomer John Collins to show the same kind of physical, pugnacious edge that defined Detroit's rise to the top of the Eastern Conference last season, Monday's NBA preseason opener between the Phoenix Suns and Detroit Pistons delivered your answer:

With the Suns holding a 13-9 lead early in the first quarter, Collins — who joined the Pistons on a three-year, $51 million contract in free agency this summer — ran to establish position in the lane. Brooks, the last Sun back on defense, stepped up to extend a not-so-warm greeting to Detroit's new power forward. As Collins worked to cross to the right block to look for an entry pass, Brooks pulled the chair and slid over to his high side, resulting in Collins falling and sliding across the floor.

As Collins started to get up, Brooks pressed right up on him, extending a forearm into the Piston's back. After Collins regained his feet and began to space out toward the right corner, Brooks extended a forearm again, this time directly into Collins' chest. (You can see Collins raising his arms out to his sides, as if to say to the officials, "You guys see this, right?")

After fellow new Piston Isaiah Joe launched a catch-and-shoot 3-pointer from the left wing, Collins started to crash the offensive glass from the corner. Brooks faced him and bodied him up to try to keep him from corralling the board. He was unsuccessful, though; after Collins came down with the rebound, Brooks swiped down at the ball with his left hand, catching Collins in the face. Eventually, Brooks wrapped Collins up with both arms, resulting in a foul call.

The whistle, however, didn't seem like quite enough of a sanction for Brooks to Collins, who chose to take matters — and Brooks' throat — into his own hands.

After players and coaches swarmed in to prevent a dust-up from turning into a donnybrook, the officials reviewed the incident and meted out discipline: a flagrant foul-1 for Collins for "contact around the neck," and a technical foul on Brooks "for his unsportsmanlike contact." The Pistons got one free throw; the Suns got two, plus possession. (Advantage: Brooks.)

Detroit won the preseason affair, 109-107 , on a game-winning layup by rookie guard Ebuka Okorie.

Brooks, who led the NBA in technical fouls last season , finished with 11 points, two rebounds and four personal fouls in 15 minutes of work in his preseason debut. Collins chipped in 10 points, three rebounds and a pair of steals in 16 minutes in his first action as a Piston — an appearance that featured the kind of action that'll likely endear him to the Detroit faithful.

"I mean, I wasn't necessarily trying to set that tone," a smiling Collins told reporters after the game. "But I'm glad I did. Sometimes, you just gotta go out there and play basketball, and the game gets physical. I'm gonna go out there and compete every night. Guys do what they do; you know, we're gonna play basketball. Can't control every aspect of the game. Just gotta go out there and hoop."

articles.title: Why LeBron James donated $2.5 million in 2016 to Muhammad Ali despite never playing the same sport
articles.summary: LeBron James pledged $2.5 million in November 2016 to the Muhammad Ali exhibit at the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and
articles.body: LeBron James pledged $2.5 million in November 2016 to the Muhammad Ali exhibit at the Smithsonian's National Museum of African American History and Culture in Washington. Maverick Carter, his business partner, was part of the gift, and it added the LeBron James Family Foundation and Carter to the museum's list of founding donors. Ali boxed and James plays basketball, so a shared sport was never the link. The 6-foot-9 forward pointed to a debt he believes every pro athlete owes. Ali had died that June at age 74.LeBron James' $2.5 million Muhammad Ali donation have little to do with basketballLeBron James announced the gift on Nov. 17, 2016, and the target was specific. The money backs "Muhammad Ali: A Force for Change," an exhibit that opened in September at the museum. The building itself had opened on Sept. 24 on the National Mall, next to the Washington Monument.The display was not a boxing showcase. It ran across the Sports Gallery and the Making A Way Out of No Way Gallery, and it included the heavyweight champion's headgear and the training robe he wore at Dundee's Fifth Street Gym. Visitors saw Ali through community activism, resistance, politics, spirituality, and culture. He also appeared in the Michael Jordan Game Changers Hall, which covered people whose actions changed their sport and the country around it.Ali's record explains the interest. In the 1960s and 1970s, he spoke against racism, raised the profile of the Nation of Islam and drew attention to the Vietnam War. After boxing, he kept working as a social activist, cultural critic and humanitarian.James said every professional athlete, no matter race or gender, "owes a huge debt of gratitude to Muhammad Ali." He placed Ali beside Jackie Robinson and Jesse Owens as figures who used sport to push civil rights forward. In his view, every generation should study that legacy.Damion Thomas, curator of the Sports Gallery, called James "the most socially active superstar in sports today." Thomas said Ali carried the racial and social tension of his era and blurred the lines between politics and sports, and between activism and entertainment.Lonnie Ali, the champion's widow, thought about children first. She said the exhibit will teach young visitors about her husband's humanitarian work and his stance on social justice for all people. She added that "if Muhammad was alive today he would be honored."How does LeBron James keep his philanthropic initiatives active through his foundation?The LeBron James Family Foundation began in 2004 with small gestures, mostly bike and backpack giveaways in Akron. It grew from there. The group moved into after-school programs for students spread across several dozen schools, then opened its own public school. As of early 2023, the school served about 575 third through eighth graders. A family resource center inside it offers mental health support, financial literacy classes, legal aid and GED courses for parents.Later, the activism shifted to housing. Down the street, the foundation provides rent-free homes for as many as 16 families when they need them, and it has plans for 50 affordable units. House Three Thirty, a community facility in Akron, is part of the same effort.In 2015, James partnered with the University of Akron to guarantee four-year scholarships for eligible students who finish high school and meet classroom and community requirements. By the time of the Ali gift, the Wheels for Education and Akron I PROMISE Network programs were serving more than 1,100 area students.Mya Smiley hailed James’ kind-hearted gesture. The University of Akron sophomore, 19 at the time, said the foundation's scholarship and counseling made college possible, and she wants to become a social worker for foster kids. James has said the program grew by "listening and responding to our community and what they need."Akron gets the focus because people there helped James and his family when he was a kid, according to foundation executive director Michele Campbell. James has said he planned to give back even before he reached the NBA.What other causes has LeBron James backed off the court?James has also used his voice. In 2010, his televised move to Miami, "The Decision," drew heavy criticism, yet it raised around $4 million for charity, a fact many people overlooked. In 2012, after Trayvon Martin's death in Florida, James tweeted a photo of Heat teammates in hoodies with their heads bowed and the hashtag WeWantJustice.In 2020 he helped lead More Than A Vote, which ran voter registration and early-vote drives and urged Black voters in particular to get to the polls. Also in 2020, after the police killing of George Floyd in Minneapolis, he joined other players in calling for an end to racial inequality and police brutality. The Ali gift landed four years after the hoodie photo and four years before that voting push.San Antonio coach Gregg Popovich has praised James for years as an example for kids with fewer advantages. Lisa Delpy Neirotti, a George Washington University sports management professor, pointed to James' goal of sending 10% of his wealth to causes and communities and called it above and beyond what most athletes aim for. James has summed up his approach by saying everything he does "has to have a purpose."How did LeBron James build his fortune through the NBA and business ventures?James has an estimated net worth of $850 million. On the court, he has won four NBA championships and become the league's all-time leading scorer. Through the 2025-26 season, he earned $581.4 million in NBA salary, the most in league history. His rookie deal with Cleveland paid $18.8 million over four years, and his last Lakers season paid $52.6 million.His 2026-27 pay looks very different. The $850 million star signed a two-year deal with the Philadelphia 76ers worth just under $8 million, with $3.88 million this season and $4.07 million next year if the option is used.He signed with Nike at 18, before playing an NBA game, on a seven-year deal worth $90 million, and he passed on more upfront money from Reebok. In 2015, Nike gave him a lifetime deal widely valued above $1 billion. Front Office Sports reported in September that Polymarket pays him $15 million a year, almost four times his 76ers salary.Ownership stakes add to the total. A stake of about 1% in Beats by Dre turned into roughly $30 million before taxes when Apple bought the company for $3 billion in 2014. In 2012, he invested less than $1 million in Blaze Pizza. In 2021, he and Carter became partners in Fenway Sports Group, which owns the Red Sox and Liverpool, among other assets.SpringHill, the media company he built with Carter, lost $17 million in 2022 and $28 million in 2023, cut staff and agreed to merge with Fulwell 73.Stay updated with the latest Asian Games 2026 news, check the Asian Games medal tally and complete Asian Games schedule.Get the latest Sports News and Live updates. articles.title: NBA insider believes the Spurs are considering starting all three of their star guards
articles.summary: The Spurs could go all-out with their starting lineup in the 2026-27 season.
articles.body:
Dylan Harper broke out as one of the San Antonio Spurs ' best players during the 2025-26 season. Considering it was his rookie season, it was natural for him to play a smaller role compared to veteran guard De'Aaron Fox and second-year standout Stephon Castle.

However, the 2026 Playoffs proved that Harper was ready for a shot at a starter spot. To start the 2026-27 season, the likely backcourt is still Fox and Castle, but it seems that the idea of starting them alongside Harper has been floating around.

The Spurs could start with all of their standout guards at the same time

In the NBA Finals against the New York Knicks , Harper was arguably the best offensive player for the Spurs . He has a natural ability to get to the rim with his speed and craftiness while also having elite finishing in his skill set.

Harper has the potential to become one of the standout offensive guards in the league. At the same time, he is also a decent defender, so he is easy to plug into a lineup. In fact, it opens up the possibility of him starting alongside his fellow guards.

Since both Harper and Castle can play bigger than usual with their length and athleticism, it is feasible to start them all together. It would be a headache for some people, but it could work out well in the end.

"It's no secret he's not going to be satisfied coming off the bench. The people in his camp aren't going to be happy. This kid, who's a potential rising superstar, wants to be in the starting lineup," Tim MacMahon said about the Spurs' guard trio on The Hoop Collective .

"They're going to have to get him in the starting lineup; I don't think it'll be at the expense of De'Aaron Fox or Stephon Castle. They'll have to start those 3 guards and figure out the rotation from there."

It is a valid point to make because the Spurs could feasibly run that trio at the same time. With Victor Wembanyama as their center, they already have the size in the paint, so playing energetic defense could help them maintain their level on either side of the floor.

articles.title: Wizards GM urges Anthony Davis to 'remind basketball world' of what he is
articles.summary: Will Dawkins, the Wizards GM, fully expects Anthony Davis to remind everyone in the NBA why he is a top 75 player of all-time.
articles.body:
Legacies are usually shaped by recency. Players who have been on the court more in the past few years tend to get more attention than those who aren't seen as often. Anthony Davis is on the other side of this coin. Many fans haven't seen him at full strength in recent seasons. In fact, his whole injury history has become a meme. Will Dawkins and the Washington Wizards plan to flip that narrative on its head in the upcoming 2026-27 NBA season. He made his expectations of the big man very clear.

Wizards GM Dawkins pressures Davis to 'remind' the NBA of what he is

Anthony Davis is healthy and ready to go in the Wizards lineup. Those are words that have been rare in the past couple of NBA seasons. Most recently, he battled through a groin injury and a finger ligament injury prior to getting traded. A year before, the big man had to deal with a detached retina and adductor strains. All of that meant he played only 71 games over the past two seasons. Wizards GM Will Dawkins plans to change all of that.

See, the Wizards are starting their ascent into becoming NBA championship contenders. They have Trae Young to set the offense. An upcoming star in AJ Dybantsa will be useful too. Beyond that, they have a strong supporting core with Bilal Coulibaly, Bub Carrington, and Khris Middleton. Davis is at the center of all that. That is why Dawkins urges the big man to remind everyone how much of a beast he is on the court after about two seasons of subpar outings, via David Aldridge and Josh Dobbins of The Athletic.

"What I will say is, AD is in a great frame of mind. He's focused and ready to start the season. I would say he's very much a motivated player right now, and I expect AD to remind the basketball world who he really is," the Wizards GM declared.

Before the plague of injuries Davis suffered over the past two seasons, he was doing great. The big man was an NBA All-Star during the 2024-25 season. A year prior, he finished fourth in Defensive Player of the Year voting and earned an All-NBA second-team nod. Due to recency bias, some fans may think that Davis can no longer turn back the clock. This is where most of them might be proven wrong in the coming months.

The former first-overall pick in the 2012 NBA Draft has a lot to give. The Wizards' roster construction also takes a lot of pressure off his shoulders. Alex Sarr can play center while Davis plays in his natural power forward spot. Young also gets the perfect pick-and-roll partner, freeing up the interior. More than that, Kyshawn George and Bilal Coulibaly have also proven themselves as capable defenders who can help Davis. When they need a spark plug, Middleton comes in to score points.

Dawkins built this team in a way that eases the burden on each player. He would not ask Davis to 'make the basketball world remember ' if the big man had no teammates who allowed him to do so in the first place.

articles.title: El Barça tilda la propuesta de la NBA de "broma"
articles.standfirst: La Euroliga decide no aceptar la oferta de la Liga estadounidense
articles.summary: La Euroliga decide no aceptar la oferta de la Liga estadounidense
articles.body: La Euroliga decidió, en Asamblea General, seguir su camino, es decir, mantener su idea de una expansión y convertir los equipos en franquicias. Ambos temas estaban en el punto del día de esa Asamblea, una de las más trascendentales en la historia de la competición. Los 13 equipos con licencia A, socios y propietarios de la competición, se reunieron a la orilla del Lago Como para decidir el futuro a corto y medio plazo de la competición. Y también para hablar de la oferta que la NBA habría hecho llegar en las negociaciones que mantienen ambos estamentos. Sin comunicación oficial al respecto, la oferta no habría salido adelante, una vez estudiada por los 13 equipos propietarios. De hecho, el medio especializado Basketnews se ha hecho eco de alguna de las reacciones de los propietarios de la Euroliga al respecto de esa propuesta de la NBA. Alguno de ellos la calificó como "inaceptable" y "colonialista" mientras otros, algo más mesurados, creen que la NBA debe mejorar significativamente su oferta para seguir adelante. Basketnews también hace referencia a la fecha de ultimátum que, al parecer, habría puesto al NBA. Esa fecha la adelantó en su momento La Gazzetta dello Sport. El 'deadline' que la NBA habría marcado para una respuesta de la Euroliga es precisamente este martes 6 de octubre, coincidiendo con la Asamblea General. Aunque la Euroliga no ha confirmado su respuesta a la NBA, todo indica que los 13 socios reunidos ni siquiera habrían tenido en cuenta la propuesta de la Liga estadounidense. Más detalles sobre estas reacciones ofrece el medio griego SDNA, al que también hace referencia Basketnews. Según ese medio, Panathinaikos, Real Madrid, Fenerbahce y Bayern estarían a favor de continuar con la negociación esperando que la NBA mejore los térmimos de su ofrecimiento. De hecho el Madrid habría pedido 30 días para que mejoren su proposición. Pero hay un sector más duro formado por equipos como el Olympiacos, el Armani Milán y el Barcelona, que se opusieron a continuar sobre la base actual de la propuesta de la NBA. De hecho, y según informa SDNA, el Barça incluso habría tildado de "broma" la proposición de la NBA. Al Lago Como en representación del Barça acudieron el presidente Joan Laporta, Xavier O'Callaghan y Sisco Pujol. Sin embargo, tal y como informa SDNA, el Olympiacos es el equipo que habría adoptado la postura más firme en contra de seguir negociando. En ese información se habla de que el actual campeón de la Euroliga habría impulsado una votación que habría puesto fin definitivamente a las conversaciones con la NBA. La petición del Olympiacos no prosperó y en su lugar los accionistas de la Euroliga optaron por continuar las negociaciones y permitir que la NBA presente una nueva oferta.
