articles.title: New Anthony Davis Rumors on Desire for New Contract After Offseason Trade Buzz
articles.summary: As Anthony Davis gets closer to making his official Washington Wizards debut eight months after being acquired in a trade, his long-term future with the club remains a big question mark.
articles.body:
As Anthony Davis gets closer to making his official Washington Wizards debut eight months after being acquired in a trade, his long-term future with the club remains a big question mark.

Per The Athletic's David Aldridge and Josh Robbins , teams around the league are "well" aware that Davis' camp wants a deal that will "pay him at, or very near, maximum salaries."

Davis is entering the final guaranteed year of his current contract with a $58.5 million salary. He also holds a $62.8 million player option for 2027-28. The 10-time All-Star has been eligible to sign an extension worth up to $275 million over four years since Aug. 6.

The Wizards acquired Davis from the Dallas Mavericks in February, but he has yet to suit up for them due to a hand injury that occurred earlier in the 2025-26 season.

Despite rumors earlier in the summer that Davis and the Wizards would talk about an extension when he became eligible, neither side appeared to be in a rush to get a deal done.

Robbins reported on Aug. 6 that no "meaningful talks" between the two sides would be held until after the season begins.

Speaking to reporters during media day on Sept. 28, Davis indicated he intends to play out this season before making a decision, at least pertaining to his player option.

"When the season is over," Davis said. "I'm going to go through the season, and kind of do what I do at a high level, and then, when it's over, you know, sit down and have those key conversations again with the front office."

Since neither Davis nor the Wizards knows how he will fit with their current core group, their decision to wait on extension talks makes sense.

Given the frequent injury issues Davis has had throughout his career, particularly in recent seasons, his desire for a max or near-max contract could be a deal-breaker for some clubs in the apron era with more attention given to who is getting big pay days than ever before.

If Davis has a season like he did in 2023-24 with the Los Angeles Lakers, when he played 76 games, made the All-NBA team and finished fourth in Defensive Player of the Year voting, it will be much easier for him to secure the type of deal he is looking for.

There hasn't been anything wrong with the way Davis has played in the two seasons since then with 23.5 points, 11.4 rebounds, 3.3 assists and 2.0 blocks per game in 71 starts.

The last number is key because Davis has only played 71 out of a possible 164 games during that period. If you start with the period when he was traded to Dallas by the Lakers, he has played 29 out of a possible 115 games.

Washington is in a good financial position to potentially handle a Davis extension if things come together for the two sides. Trae Young is the only player currently on the team who will earn more than $16 million during the 2027-28 season.

If AJ Dybantsa becomes the player Washington hopes, any extension for him wouldn't kick in until the 2030-31 season. Young's current deal will be expired by that time; and Davis would be going into the final year of his deal, assuming he were to sign a four-year contract.

It's so far down the road to be thinking that big picture, but this Wizards roster is one of the most fascinating in the Eastern Conference because of the pieces in place.

Young did get some run with the Wizards last season after he was acquired from the Atlanta Hawks in January, but it was only a five-game sample size before he was shut down.

The Wizards won the lottery to take Dybantsa with the No. 1 pick in the 2026 draft. He joins a core with Young, Davis, Bub Carrington, Bilal Coulibaly and Alex Sarr.

There's a lot of of interesting pieces in that group that everyone in Washington wants to see play together.

Davis can be a difference-maker for any team because of his two-way ability. If he helps lift the Wizards back to relevance, his leverage for the deal he wants will dramatically increase.

The San Antonio Spurs have one of the deepest rosters in the NBA, but they reportedly already know the hierarchy behind star center Victor Wembanyama.

articles.title: Angel Reese's Dream Make Full-Time Move to Hawks' State Farm Arena amid Massive Attendance Growth
articles.summary: The Atlanta Dream are moving into a bigger arena full-time amid soaring attendance numbers.
articles.body:
The Atlanta Dream are moving into a bigger arena full-time amid soaring attendance numbers.

The team announced Tuesday that the Dream will play all 25 of its 2027 home games at State Farm Arena in Atlanta, the home of the NBA's Hawks, as the WNBA schedule expands to 50 games.

According to a press release from the Dream, the move "reflects the unprecedented growth of the franchise, increasing ticket demand and overall excitement for the entire Dream fan experience."

The team has seen a 400 percent increase in season-ticket members over the last five years and now has ticket buyers from all 50 states. It has also had 65 sellout games over the past three years, including eight sold-out games at State Farm Arena.

"This is an exciting next chapter for the Atlanta Dream, and a direct reflection of the exciting style of play that is Dream basketball, the passion of our fans and the incredible growth of this franchise," said Morgan Shaw Parker, president and COO of the Atlanta Dream. "Our players and our fans have transformed Gateway Center Arena into the most exciting experience in the WNBA. State Farm Arena gives us the opportunity to welcome thousands of additional fans while creating an even bigger stage for women's basketball in Atlanta. We look forward to bringing the energy, traditions and spirit of Gateway with us to the heart of our city."

According to The Athletic's Annie Costabile , the team practices at the CORE4 Athletic Complex in Chamblee, Ga., which is about 31 miles away from their former arena, Gateway Center Arena, and 15 miles away from State Farm Arena.

The Dream are not expected to return to the complex next year but have not announced plans for a new practice facility yet.

During the 2026 campaign, the WNBA drew a league-record 3.79 million fans to its games, according to David Broughton of the Sports Business Journal, representing a 20 percent year-over-year increase. The Dream had a 54.7 percent increase in games at their home venue, ranking second in the league with an average attendance of 96 percent.

Part of the reason for the increase was the league's decision to move 25 of its games into larger venues. Those games drew 388,997 fans and averaged 15,743, marking a 40 percent increase over the average of the games played in typical arenas.

The Dream beat the Washington Mystics in the first round of the WNBA playoffs and took down the New York Liberty in Game 1 of the semifinals. The two teams will meet at State Farm Arena for Game 2 on Wednesday.

articles.title: LeBron James Reportedly Let Joel Embiid 'Hear It' After Being 'Minutes' Late to 76ers Practice
articles.summary: LeBron James reportedly let Joel Embiid "hear it" during a recent Philadelphia 76ers practice after Embiid was late to the session, according to NBA broadcaster Mike Breen.
articles.body:
LeBron James reportedly let Joel Embiid "hear it" during a recent Philadelphia 76ers practice after Embiid was late to the session, according to NBA broadcaster Mike Breen .

During Monday night's broadcast of the preseason clash between the 76ers and New York Knicks, Breen revealed that "somebody" told him about the encounter before the game.

"They were out ready to practice, Joel Embiid walked out on the court a couple of minutes late and LeBron let him hear it," Breen reported.

LeBron James Gets Trolled by Michael Che

James and Embiid are entering their first year as teammates following a busy offseason in which the 76ers added Jaylen Brown and the NBA's all-time leading scorer to a core that includes Tyrese Maxey, VJ Edgecombe and Embiid.

While Embiid remains a dominant offensive force for Philadelphia when healthy, his punctuality has been an issue in the past.

In Nov. 2024, Maxey reportedly criticized Embiid for being late "for everything" and "challenged" him to be on time for team activities moving forward.

As for James, he's known for his meticulous workout regimen in order to prepare for each season. That hasn't changed entering his 24th year in the NBA, as Edgecombe reflected on the first time he saw James in the locker room before practice.

"He was in there before everybody," Edgecombe said, per ESPN's Dave McMenamin . "As usual."

With expectations high for the 76ers entering their 2026-27 campaign, James has prioritized accountability among his new teammates.

"The only thing that matters is what we preach every day and how we're gonna hold each other accountable," James said during a Sept. 25 episode of his Mind the Game podcast.

The 76ers have three more preseason games ahead of them before they open the regular season against the Knicks on Oct. 20.

articles.title: 2026-27 NBA Season Preview: Thunder, Nuggets, Timberwolves, Trail Blazers, Jazz (Northwest Division)
articles.summary: Let's break down what to like and be concerned about, a lineup to watch and a reasonable range for each team to finish in the standings.
articles.body:
With the regular season set to tip off on Oct. 20, let's take a look at where each team in the Northwest Division stands. We'll break down what to like and be concerned about, a lineup to watch and a reasonable range for them to finish in the standings.

Back-to-back MVPs don't grow on trees, especially guards that can convert over 60% of their 2s on midrange heavy diets. There's an inevitability I've come to appreciate with SGA. He moves at his own pace — moves you at his own pace — en route to an endless supply of fancy finishes and midrange goodness. He's been lifting defensively-slanted lineups for years now, and still has relatively low-hanging fruit (hello, 3-point volume) to grab.

This defense, headlined by Chet Holmgren (he's still really good, y'all!), should remain absurd. A healthier version of Jalen Williams will boost what is already an elite unit, and I'm excited to see how Cason Wallace builds on his first All-Defense campaign. Isaiah Hartenstein rounds out the (projected) starting five as one of the more underrated defenders in the league. Alex Caruso remains an absolute madman, and would be a mainstay for All-Defensive teams if he played more. Jaylin Williams is equal parts scheme-versatile and charge magnet. Good luck scoring against this unit. Again.

While I expect Wallace to step into Lu Dort's starting spot, I wouldn't be surprised if OKC rolled with Ajay Mitchell to add more of a scoring punch. He's dynamic with the ball in his hands, making him an ideal option to either destroy defenses that are tilted by SGA, or pose enough of a threat to further unlock SGA as an off-ball option.

As a longtime Kenrich Williams enjoyer, I'm so glad he's still on this roster. Consummate professional who can step in and fill just about any role you need him to. He'll forever have a fan here.

BIGGEST QUESTION MARK: Non-SGA half-court creation

There are only so many things you can poke at for a team this good, but I would like to feel a little better about the non-SGA options as a whole — at least through a playoff context.

Teams continue to stash wings on Holmgren; at some point, he has to take that gambit off the board for good. Last year was an injury-riddled campaign for Jalen Williams, but the shots he generates for himself against high-level defenses can leave a little to be desired.

This could be as simple as Williams getting and staying healthy, Mitchell continuing to win as a secondary, and Holmgren making strides against smaller defenders. Heck, a full season of Jared McCain — paired with some needed inside-the-arc growth — could go a long way.

In light of Isaiah Joe's departure specifically, I am once again keeping an eye on the 3-point shooting of OKC. McCain feels like the Thunder's only trustworthy, high-volume guy that teams will care about. I wonder how players will draw consistent hard close-outs by the time we reach the playoffs.

More of a curiosity than concern, but in what ways (if any) will the Thunder miss Lu Dort? There is something to say about his brand of physicality and what it did from a culture-setting standpoint; he was also someone more than willing to take on the big wing assignments if called upon. The lineup data certainly suggests they won't miss him, but I want to see how seamless this transition is.

Also more of a curiosity note, but I wonder how much we'll see from the rookie scale guys aside from McCain. A reasonable year of health would suggest we don't see much of Bennett Stirtz or Aday Mara, but I sure would like to.

LINEUP TO WATCH: SGA-Wallace-Caruso-Jal.Williams-Holmgren

Put this at the top of my Closing Lineup Intrigue list. This group has played 37 minutes together since the 2024-25 season, and they've won those minutes by 45 points. I don't expect them to continue shooting 50% from 3 as a unit, but this is a very fun mix of scoring, screening, and absurd defense.

They have the best guard, if not player, in the NBA. They have an elite defense. They have a top-three-at-worst coach in the NBA in Mark Daigneault. If they were the 1-seed while suffering through one of the most injury-riddled campaigns in the league last year, a healthier version should absolutely flirt with 70 wins again.

An injury to SGA could certainly hurt their ceiling, but the Thunder went 8-6 without SGA last year while dealing with a host of other injuries in the process. It's hard to overstate how strong this team is, foundationally. That defense travels; most importantly, it turns you over — which should lessen the strain on their half-court offense.

WHAT TO LIKE: Nikola Jokić and Jamal Murray, making music

There's room to argue if Nikola Jokić is still the league's best player — SGA and Victor Wembanyama in particular have strong cases to make, and there are guys in Los Angeles and Miami that would proudly raise their hands. At the very least, Jokić is the league's most dominant offensive player — a historically efficient scorer that doubles as arguably the best passer in the league.

Jamal Murray is dynamic in his own right, an audacious pull-up threat who's more than comfortable operating inside the arc when he needs to. Together, they've created the league's most difficult two-man game to stop. Traditional ball screens, handoffs, inverted actions with Jokić handling — it all throws opponents for a loop.

There is no good answer for any of it; you can only hope that Murray doesn't have the juice to get downhill, or that Jokić settles for (and misses) 3s off the pop (something to monitor).

It's been a blast watching Aaron Gordon evolve during his time in Denver. He's an absolute monster in the dunker spot, has enough on-ball juice to win against size mismatches, has turned himself into a reliable shooter (41.3% from 3 over the past two seasons) and can toggle between handling tough on-ball assignments and plugging gaps off the ball defensively. "Star in his role" is a lot more fitting than "role player" when he's upright.

I'm much more "in" on DeMar DeRozan as a super sub that can close when you need him, versus DeRozan as a locked-in starter that you need a particular context around to maximize. He's still an efficient, somewhat schemeproof bucket-getter with underrated playmaking chops. He's more than capable of soaking up usage in the dreaded non-Jokić minutes; depending on how the other reserves perform, DeRozan's presence may allow the Nuggets to take a page out of the Las Vegas Aces' book and rest both Jokić and Murray at the same time to fully maximize their impact together.

It's unreasonable to be fully "in" on a guy based on preseason action, so I'll just say I enjoyed watching Alpha Diallo defend — including a forced eight-second violation — and I'm excited to see more of him.

BIGGEST QUESTION MARK: Defensive consistency

Same as it ever was: the Nuggets need to hit a certain level defensively to complement what should be another elite offensive season. Can they find the right coverage mixture for Jokić, and will he give more consistent effort than we saw last season? Will Gordon be on the floor enough, and can he reach near All-Defense levels? What level of navigation will we get from this cast of guards and wings? How much zone will David Adelman throw out?

There's a roadmap to average, but it's on them to nail it.

I'm on record liking the Marvin Bagley signing, I have Da'Ron Holmes intrigue, and I still have some Zeke Nnaji stock hidden in an undisclosed location (I know, I know), but there's certainly a level of "prove it" with the non-Jokić options. We know that Gordon-at-the-5 is Denver's best look; the regular season has to be spent making sure that, come playoff time, it isn't the only look that'll work.

The Nuggets and Celtics have long been at the opposite end of the "Elite Offense But Also…" coin for me. The Celtics have gotten it done with rim rates that makes me cringe; the Nuggets have gotten it done with 3-point rates that makes me cringe, though they did jump from 30th to 17th (!) last season. Hopefully they continue to work toward balancing things out, though the DeRozan signing doesn't breed a ton of confidence in the 3-point rate specifically.

I think there's a pathway to the Nuggets being "fine" on defense overall, but boy do I wish they could turn teams over. You'd have to go back to the title year (2022-23) for the last time they weren't in the bottom-10 of opponent turnover rate — and they were 18th that year.

LINEUP TO WATCH: Murray-Braun-DeRozan-Gordon-Jokić

DeRozan is already slated to come off the bench. I hope whatever discussions led to that revelation also came with notice that closing minutes aren't guaranteed. There's absolutely a world where the starting group (Cam Johnson in for DeRozan) is simply their best lineup, and thus, the lineup they close games with more often.

Jokić having two prolific shotmakers to run two-man-game with is tantalizing if the defense can hold up enough. If teams lean more toward switching Murray-Jokić stuff — which certainly isn't a foolproof answer, but it's a trend I'm monitoring — DeRozan's ability to create may hold a little more value than Johnson's shooting within that context.

Despite the injuries they suffered, the Nuggets still managed to post a top-three offensive rating in NBA history, per Cleaning the Glass. The Jokić-Murray duo guarantees an incredibly high floor. If the Nuggets are actually solid in the non-Jokić minutes this year and take a step forward defensively, it's not hard to map out a pathway to winning 60+ games.

There are obvious injury concerns to point to, most notably with Gordon as an important, impactful glue piece on both ends of the floor. To the on-court product, if the bench underwhelms and the defense is once-again rudderless, they're going to struggle to lock up a top-six seed.

WHAT TO LIKE: LaMelo Ball-Anthony Edwards backcourt

Anthony Edwards has established himself as one of the most lethal offensive players we have in the league. He's a devastating downhill threat, a growing midrange and back-to-basket scorer, and one of the best pull-up shooters from deep that we have in the league. He's put in a lot of work to etch the outline of a three-level scorer, and he's done even more work to leverage that growth into forcing teams to put two-on-the-ball against him.

Giving him LaMelo Ball as a backcourt partner feels like a match made in basketball heaven.

Ball is one of the most creative playmakers we have in the league, one willing to push the pace more often than Edwards has shown to be. The hit-aheads and general pick-and-roll work should give Edwards more opportunities to attack tilted defenses instead of being tasked with doing the titling.

Ball's willingness to bomb away from 3, and from very far out, should give Edwards more room to work with as a driver. And where Ball has room to grow as a rim- or paint presence, Edwards' ability to get downhill should tilt defenses in a way that Ball will benefit from.

Jaden McDaniels is one of the best perimeter defenders in the league, fantastic against wings and more than willing to hound much-smaller guards and make their lives miserable. On the other end, he's continued to grow as a closeout attacker and overall shot creator. In a context where he should consistently be defended by a team's third- or fourth-best defender, he could shine pretty bright. Do not be surprised if he's in (fringe) All-Star conversations.

Dread it. Run from it. Rudy Gobert's rim protection arrives all the same. Every year, players show (or outwardly discuss) a lack of respect for Gobert. And every year, teams struggle to score at the rim when he contests shots, and they take a lower share of their shots at the rim when Gobert's on the floor. He's been a walking top-10 defense for over a decade at this point.

I'm just a huge fan of the speed, chaos, and 3-point shooting Ayo Dosunmu injected into this group post-trade last year, and especially in the playoffs. Three-"guard" lineups with him, Ball and Edwards should be fun to watch.

BIGGEST QUESTION MARK: The non-Rudy Gobert minutes

Here is your obligatory "What are the non-Rudy Gobert minutes going to look like?" mention. In Gobert's four seasons in Minnesota, the Wolves have been nearly five points per 100 possessions better with him on the floor, with that difference almost solely coming on the defensive end.

I am excited to see more Joan Beringer this year, but there's a good bit of pressure for him to be immediately steady. I'm rooting for it to work; I just need to see it work.

Quietly, the Wolves saw switches against pick-and-rolls at one of the highest rates in the league. Their efficiency against those looks left a bit to be desired, to be kind. There's a lot of pick-and-roll goodness to be had with this group, but I do wonder what their process and overall shot quality will look like when they face defenses with the personnel to cross-match and ultimately flatten them out. I am looking at you, Mr. Ball and Mr. Edwards. Speaking of which …

At their best and most attentive, Ball and Edwards are both gifted at reading passing lanes, poking at handles, and ultimately turning teams over. At their worst, you can catch them flat-footed or generally disinterested, opening up cuts and relocations that fracture the integrity of a defense. Those two need to be more consistent off-ball defenders for the Wolves to hit their full potential. They're physically capable.

It's definitely fair to argue that swapping out Julius Randle and Naz Reid for LaMelo Ball and Jonathan Kuminga will make the Wolves better overall. I do think it's fair to point out that you lose a good deal of collective physicality with that swap, and it's worth monitoring how impactful (and where) that could be.

LINEUP TO WATCH: Ball-Edwards-Dosunmu-McDaniels-Gobert

The Edwards-Dosunmu-McDaniels-Gobert quartet played 120 minutes together last season, but they were outscored by 51 points in that span. Is replacing Julius Randle (-36 in group-high 57 minutes as the 5th) with Ball enough to tilt the scales? You technically get smaller, but you get a major boost in pace, playmaking, and 3-point volume.

The defense should be quite good, if not elite — especially if there's consistent buy-in from Ball and Edwards. And with Ball and Edwards at the forefront on the other end, there's a pathway to the Wolves having a top-five offense — if not the best offense in the league.

There's a world where the increased pace accentuates the questionable decision-making that can pop up with Ball and Edwards. That, plus opposing defenses leaning into a higher dosage of switching could lead to a good-but-underwhelming offensive season as a whole. If their defense is closer to 10th (or worse), it's a formula that could have the Wolves winning 45-48 games rather than flirting with (or even eclipsing) 60.

If nothing else, the Blazers have plenty of options to cycle through this year!

Ja Morant is here , looking to reclaim his status as a top-tier guard while adding more driving juice to a team that gets downhill quite a bit. Damian Lillard is back, hopefully prepared to provide a much-needed injection of (off-the-bounce) shooting for a Blazers team that needs it.

Scoot Henderson returns after … maybe not a full-blown shift in role, but at least a notable one as an off-ball attacker. There's also Jrue Holiday, who's more of a 6-foot-4 basketball player than a guard in a traditional sense. He'll run the offense, attack tilted defenses, ramp up his 3-point volume when called upon, and will face-guard the electronic device you're reading this on if you ask him to.

The defensive trio of Holiday, Toumani Camara, and Donovan Clingan is one of my favorites — and, frankly, one of the best in the league. Holiday and Camara can defend 1-through-4, while Clingan has established himself as one of the best interior defenders in the league. I'm excited to watch them work.

I don't know how much it'll carry over this year in light of the roster and sideline changes, but boy did I enjoy the amount of full-court pressure the Blazers tossed out last season. Looking at what Alex Sarama did with the Portland Fire on the WNBA side, I hope this just becomes a Portland basketball staple.

I was surprised the Blazers were able to keep Robert Williams III, but what a luxury it is to have him coming off the bench. Not many teams can match the 48 minutes of rim protection the Blazers can toss out between him and Clingan.

While I generally like the guard room in a vacuum, figuring out a cohesive rotation that features all of them is well above my paygrade. If new head coach Micah Nori is truly going to split Morant and Lillard — which, for defensive purposes, makes a ton of sense — how are these combinations going to shake out?

And in general, can you find the right combinations of shooting, playmaking, and defense to truly make this work?

I just … virtually every bit of Blazers news I've read this summer has made me sigh, and I'm not even a Blazers fan. The shameful contract given to/accepted by Nori, the volume of lost jobs in different facets of the organization, the play-by-play hiring and immediate firing, on-the-record comments from new owner Tom Dundon that seem to, at the very least, lack a level of empathy you'd like to see or hear. I just don't like the vibes around the organization right now, and I hope it flips when games are actually played.

I liked the way Clingan was moved around last year, but he needs to take a pretty substantial step as a ball-screen partner and finisher, especially with the guards in the room.

With Shaedon Sharpe out for the foreseeable future, what exactly is the wing/forward rotation behind first-time All-Star Deni Avdija? Jerami Grant is in Memphis. Matisse Thybulle is in LA. I'm a Vit Krejci guy, but I don't know if I want him to be this important at work.

LINEUP TO WATCH: Morant-Lillard-Holiday-Camara-Williams III

The Holiday/Camara/Williams III trio, with Avdija on the bench, was quietly +30 in 139 minutes together last season. That's a strong foundation defensively, which should, in theory, make the Morant-Lillard backcourt more viable to play. I want to see this one.

If they're able to at least flirt with being a top-10 unit defensively this year, the added offensive firepower could give them a higher floor than people are giving them credit for.

WORST CASE: Outside of the Play-In Tournament

I think it would take some real injury misfortune for the Blazers to be in worst-in-the-conference/league territory. Still, there's definitely a world where the defense takes a hit in light of their smaller backcourt and they don't score efficiently enough to offset that dip.

Similar to the Grizzlies, I'm pretty bullish on the amount of levers this team can pull. Will Hardy is a creative offensive mind with spacing principles I enjoy.

There's guard creation to like with Keyonte George and newcomer Darryn Peterson, with both having a level of on- and off-ball utility that can be useful. Lauri Markkanen has long been moved around the board because of the threat of his shooting, and he showcased some real juice as a driver (and foul-drawer) last year. Jaren Jackson Jr. is a fun inside-out threat, and you can invert the offense with Jusuf Nurkic because of his passing ability.

I'm excited to see what Ace Bailey looks like in Year 2. His in-season growth flew a little under the radar last year, but in general I like the way he was utilized. So many of his touches started with movement; with more spacing and talent around him, the context should be even easier for him.

To the rest of the bench: Isaiah Collier drives all over the place; Svi Mykhailiuk is a good shooter with underrated passing chops. Josh Okogie is willing to guard just about anyone, and is quietly coming off the best 3-point shooting season (38.5% on 2.1 attempts) of his career. If Brice Sensabaugh doesn't do anything else, he'll shoot the leather off the ball. Kyle Filipowski can be, and has been, used in a multitude of ways offensively. There's a good bit to play with here.

For whatever you can take from preseason action, it was notable to me that the Jazz opted to start in a zone look against the Nuggets in their opener. You could see the seeds of them forcing deeper-in-clock possessions, passing off assignments and working through scram switches. You could also see how perilous things felt when their guards got poked at, and the rotations behind their help weren't crisp.

There are fun lineups they can get to — do not be surprised if Okogie becomes more important at work than expected — but ultimately they have to get this defense to "serviceable" to complement the offense. They were 29th in defensive rating, per Cleaning The Glass, last year; what does this look like if they're, say, 18th?

If Nurkic misses any amount of substantial time — he's missed at least 20 games in six of the last seven seasons, so history suggests he will — I am pretty worried about the rebounding of this group.

Hardy does a great job of scheming things up and simplifying reads, but this isn't a great passing roster overall. Like, Nurk is probably one of the three or four best passers on the team. I'm curious to see how that reality plays out, and which teams (or coverages) put that under the microscope.

LINEUP TO WATCH: George-Peterson-Bailey-Markkanen-Jackson Jr.

I can hear all of Memphis yelling. I hear y'all. Jaren at the 5 is not ideal because of the rebounding (and fouling) woes. I've seen it, and I've seen the numbers. I don't think we're going to get a ton of this look, which is why Nurkic and, to a lesser extent, Jaxson Hayes are on this roster.

I don't think we're getting zero minutes of that look, though, and I'm curious to see how often we get this group together. In theory, that's a lot of shot creation and a level of collective size 3-through-5 that should allow a baseline level of switching.

The offense projects to be a multifaceted one. They have pick-and-roll creators, off-ball options, mismatch hunters, and a head coach in Hardy who can dial up some schematic fun. If the defense can be serviceable — Jackson Jr. + switchable size could provide a roadmap there — people shouldn't be too surprised by them churning out wins.

I can't rule out the defense being such a disappointment that the offensive juice is rendered moot, especially with the firepower they'll have to deal with in this division — on top of the conference itself.
